He’s Britain’s best-known progressive presenter. A fearless freedom fighter in a world of right-wing shock-jocks. Champion of the misrepresented. Defender of the underdog. Cool dad and indisputably kind.
I’m a massive fan.
So why does James O’Brien – LBC’s most listened-to host – lose all his strength when going anywhere near the biggest civil rights campaign of our age? The topic crying out for his attention: Trans rights.
This seems to be his Kryptonite.
In a recent interview with The Guardian’s Tim Jonze to publicise his new book How They Broke Britain, James said: ‘So if someone believes they were born in the wrong body, I don’t want to call them a liar. And if somebody believes their personal security is threatened by that person using the same amenities that they use, I don’t want to call them a liar either.’
Head in the sand. Look the other way. Switzerland.
James, this is so disappointing to hear. You can’t just fence sit on a human rights issue like this.
There is no equivalence between the 0.2% trans population over the age of 16 in England and Wales – according to the last census – simply looking to lead a normal life and the mighty forces lined up against us.
It’s like the end of Butch Cassidy and The Sundance Kid. We’re outnumbered by canons and Gatlin guns. We could do with an extra gunslinger or superhero saddling up and riding out to the rescue.
James, as someone who listens to you every day getting all the topics right, I can’t believe you get the subject of trans so wrong.
There has never been a trans crime wave in history. There has never been a spate of non-trans predators dressing up as women to attack others. There has never been a trans champion dominating any sport at any level.
As far as I’ve seen, it’s just one-off sporadic wins at college meetings or park runs that are blown out of all proportion by right-wing trombones. With cisgender competitors quickly resuming their place at the top.
Self-ID, the principle that a trans person can change gender markers without going through a number of administrative and medical hoops, exists in countries all over the world.
Of the countries that have introduced self-ID, none of the scare stories about widespread threats to women have come to pass – with Victor Madrigal-Borloz, UN independent expert on LGBT+ rights, stating last year that ‘350 million people live in systems of legal recognition based on self-determination, and there is not, to my knowledge, one single administrative or judicial finding that this system is actually abused by predatory males.’

Looking at my birth mum’s Facebook page, aged 15, I felt incredibly loved.
Though my dad disguised her name as he didn’t feel the time was right for me to know all the details about her, he wanted me to see my birth mum’s page.
He wanted me to know that she had listed my name and my date of birth, describing herself as a mother of four children.
It meant that I knew, when I first met her and her family in February at the age of 16, that she had kept me in mind the entire time we’d been apart.
And next year, less than two years since we reconnected, I will proudly walk her down the aisle as she marries her partner.
My sister, Gracie and I have always known we were adopted. I was adopted at 5 years old and she was adopted at 18 months.
But I’ve always felt like I have two families, and that’s something I am really proud of.
There’s never been any bad blood – my adoptive parents have always spoken very positively about my birth family – so it has never felt anything other than normal, whatever that is!
As a family we’ve always been open and honest about it and I openly shared it with people at school. It’s a part of my life and it makes me feel unique, I’d never want to hide it.
Even so, for as long as I can remember, I wanted to get in contact with my birth mum.
I kept asking my mum and dad outright when I could meet her.
To be fair, it was an ongoing discussion with them and they were always open to it when they felt the time was right.
But whenever I asked my parents to share what my birth surname was so I could look up relatives on Facebook, they’d urge me to be patient. To trust that they would share full details when I was older.
As much as I wanted to know, I understood why they were holding back and I was always confident that they would support me when that time came.
While I waited, my dad showed me my birth-mum’s Facebook page, hiding her name.
But about four months later, I came across my birth surname in my memory box – a collection of important items from before and after my adoption.
It was like finding treasure and I must have traced over that social work report a hundred times. I just couldn’t believe my eyes.

Almost a month later, having finally built up the courage, I typed in her name and I instantly recognised the Facebook page dad had shown me.
I was nervous – this was the first time I’d looked her up on my own – but excited too. I knew I could have done it with my parents, but I wanted to do it by myself. It felt important, somehow.
As much as I wanted to message her though, I didn’t. This was partly due to nerves but also, I was studying for my GCSE’s, and I had a lot going on in my life, so instead I decided to wait another couple of months.
I’ll never forget the night I finally reached out. I’d had an argument with my dad about tidying my room and needing to study harder.
Typical teenage stuff but I was really annoyed. In my angst I decided I wanted to get back at him, so I decided to contact my birth mum.
But when I began writing, I felt really confused.
I realised that I wanted to reach out to her, but that I wanted to do it with my dad. I started crying and asked him for his help.
We made up and he cuddled me as we talked it through, all of which helped me to make sense of my emotions. He even helped me write my first message to her.
‘Hello, it is me, Callum, your son.’ I typed. ‘I have wanted to say hello for so long, so, here I am!’
She responded immediately and I was so excited. She said she had longed to be in touch and was so pleased to hear from me. Her response made me feel at ease.
I felt wanted. I felt loved.
We messaged for the rest of the night, and the conversation flowed as if we had always been in touch.
Alongside, my mum and dad messaged her to say they knew I’d got in touch and that I had their full support, which helped reassure everyone. And after that, we messaged each other daily, and spoke often.
Three months later we met in person for the first time in forever.
Dad came with me for support and it put my mind at ease knowing that he had met her when I was adopted.
I then spent two full days with my birth mum, her partner and their two children – it was incredible to learn I had new siblings! And I also met my aunt and godmother.
We spent our time going through photos and talking about when we were a family.
Mum reminded me of the times we had spent playing in the park together with my grandma, and my aunty. We also talked about our lives now, learning things about each other and having fun.
She also explained why she had found it difficult to look after me, why I needed to be adopted, and that she knew it was the best place for me after meeting my adopted parents.
You might expect it to have felt strange after all this time, but it was quite the opposite. Being with them all felt very normal and natural.
When my dad came to collect me, he thanked my birth mum for looking after me, and he was clearly touched when she said how wonderful it had been spending time with me.
On the way home, he listened intently as I relayed stories of my early childhood, and of what my family is doing now. I just felt happy.
Mum and I stayed connected, messaging and ringing each other daily. Then a few months later, she asked if I would walk her down the aisle.
The request took me totally by surprise but I was dead chuffed that she’d asked me.
I was so excited, in fact, that I immediately got my parents out of bed to tell them the good news, and to ask if it was OK with them.
Thankfully, they were both very supportive, and said I should do it, if I wanted to.
I messaged her back straightaway. ‘It would be a great honour to walk you down the aisle Mum.’ I said and I really am so pleased she is marrying such an amazing man.
My mum even went the extra mile and said that my adopted parents would be welcome to attend if it makes it easier for me. That was a really lovely touch.
Now, the countdown to the wedding day in October 2024 has begun. I don’t really know what to expect as it will be my first wedding – my biggest concerns are whether my prom suit will still fit me, and if I’ll have to make a speech – but either way, I can’t wait.
Since finding out I was adopted, I always wanted to be in touch with my birth family and I am so pleased to have been able to build a relationship with them as a teenager.
While I do wish I could have met my mum sooner, reconnecting with her now has felt nothing but normal.
I now understand that she couldn’t look after me when I was little, that doesn’t make her a bad person, she was just in a challenging situation. But it does make me think adoption should be more open from the beginning.
The temptation to connect with a birth family for adopted kids like me is almost constant, but my advice is that you should always do so with your adopted parents’ knowledge.
That way everyone is involved, and things can go as smoothly as they have for me.
It may have been a long road, but I know I am truly lucky that I have two families, and am loved and supported by them both.

https://metro.co.uk/2023/10/19/jeremy-cl.title: Jeremy Clarkson is the farming hero Countryfile never was
https://metro.co.uk/2023/10/19/jeremy-cl.text:
As the BBC’s Countryfile has failed to represent British farmers for decades, Jeremy Clarkson has emerged in recent years as somewhat of a hero in rural circles – and that could be a problem.
When he swanned onto Amazon Prime in 2021 with his series, Clarkson’s Farm, it was an instant hit.
For those unaware about the premise of the show, the ex-Top Gear presenter, 63, comically struggles to make just about any profit from his newly-purchased – and aptly named – Diddly Squat Farm in the Cotswolds.
He’s dumbstruck by the seemingly impossible hurdles many people within the agriculture industry have grappled with in private for decades – and proudly broadcasts his struggles to the world.
Farmers up and down the country immediately rejoiced in the series, with James Rebanks – author of The Shepherd’s Life – famously saying Clarkson has ‘done more for farmers in one series of Clarkson’s Farm than Countryfile achieved in 30 years’.
‘There were silly bits,’ Rebanks admitted, chatting when the first series aired in 2021. ‘But in the farming community they are just delighted that someone high profile would stick up for them or have any kind of genuine empathy.’
As a farmer’s daughter, I love seeing the industry spotlighted like this.
But it worries me that a man who went on a vile, sexist tirade about Meghan Markle is now the hero of a community I was born into. And a male-dominated one, at that.
Indeed, when I posed a Clarkson’s Farm vs BBC’s Countryfile question to a British farming Facebook group, the consensus was clear with favour for the former.
‘No comparison,’ said one. ‘A lot of time for Adam [Henson, of Countryfile] but he has barely 5 minutes in the half hour and never shows his f*** ups or the real and palpable stress of the job.’
Clarkson’s Farm is refreshingly transparent because it showcases the TV star protagonist’s agricultural ineptitude. It instead champions Kaleb Cooper – a normal long-suffering country lad tasked with making it all work – who is now a breakout star of the series with 2million Instagram followers. Putting relatable and very real people to the heart of the series was clearly well-received by the community.
Someone else commented on my Facebook post: ‘Several non-farming friends have said about how Clarkson shows how hard the job can be, the weather dependency of drilling and harvest and the fine margins we work on. No one ever says they’ve seen anything interesting on Countryfile.’
I have to agree. Countryfile is primarily a show about the countryside, with a sprinkling of farming fluff, but when I see it mentioned on the show, it achieves not much more than a woolly, sanitised version of reality.
I’ve worked many lambing seasons over the years and the truth of this time of year is genuinely gruelling.
It reeks of death and afterbirth gunk truly gets everywhere. As does s**t. This is before you have the joy of putting your hand up a struggling sheep in the hope of coaxing out a massive single lamb that simply won’t budge.
Then you have to get the vet out. That’ll be your monthly profit, please.
If a lamb dies, its corpse is often skinned for an orphan to wear in an attempt to trick a mother into thinking it’s hers. Some lambs are born dead, as you discover on pulling out a rotten leg from a bleating ewe. It’s grim.
Then you’ve got the weather to contend with. One year, I remember floods so bad even fully grown ewes drowned, while many lambs were left floating, lifeless, down rivers. It was the antithesis of springtime promise. For crops, the same anxiety-inducing torment comes from the unpredictability of harvest.
With the huge unexpected overheads, economic uncertainty and generally having to be totally at the mercy of the great British weather while encountering death around every turn: farming is no breeze. But someone has to do it, if we want to eat.
Given that Clarkson shows some of these realities – and the stark contrast to Countryfile’s Disney-adult version of it – I don’t blame agri folk for god-worshipping him. He is seemingly their only mainstream cheerleader who is speaking their language.
As ground-breaking as the show is, filming has wrapped up for season three of Clarkson’s Farm and knowing that the agriculture industry will soon be tucking into the new season like a hearty pie, savouring every joke, I feel uneasy.
Although I do not blame them for it, I don’t like seeing a community I grew up in celebrating a man who epitomises many things I think are wrong with the world.
He should not be a figure to rally behind for anyone, especially after his gross, misogynistic words in one particular column for The Sun. In it, he described how he dreamt about Meghan Markle parading the streets naked, while the public shout shame and throw excrement at her.

After the article became the most complained-about ever at Ipso – with tens of thousands of write-ins – it was removed online. Clarkson later apologised, as did the publication.
Let’s not forget his other controversies. In 2020 he joked about a woman in a burka falling over and exposing a ‘red G-string and stockings’ and four years later he apparently mumbled the N word in a Top Gear outtake while reciting a nursery rhyme. He apologised saying he was ‘horrified’ that it sounded as though he had used it.

But that’s exactly what happens when a part of society isn’t truly seen and represented in the mainstream: they latch onto the loudest spokesperson they have.
Agriculture employs almost half a million people in the UK, and produces half the food we eat. It’s also estimated that 70% of the British countryside is farmland in some way.

This dearth of representation means that some folk are so quick to defend him – even his ugliest comments – because he’s the only high profile person sticking up for them. That’s dangerous. Especially for women in the industry.
That is why I am worried about a fossil like Jeremy Clarkson capturing the community’s imagination. I don’t want young farmers to get stuck on a prehistoric hill with him, repeating his sexist rhetoric, all because he’s the only one taking their plight seriously on TV.
I hope the love for Clarkson’s Farm doesn’t run this deep.
That said, I believe Amazon Prime should keep Clarkson’s Farm going – despite controversy. Representing the community is important and he’s the only one doing it properly.
Besides, Clarkson would only become a martyr if his show is axed and our community’s only mouthpiece – however controversial – is taken away. Countryfile is too out of touch with British farmers to ever truly represent them as Clarkson has.
Rather than erasing the only popular hero in this field – literally – we need to find better ones. We need more Kalebs to be championed in mainstream media who can eclipse the Clarkson effect.
We need a version of Countryfile that truly reflects farming’s reality – and that actually is about farming – without its urban-sanitised filter.
Perhaps some members of the farming community don’t want another public figure, and see Clarkson as the embodiment of farming Britain. Perhaps they chortle along to Clarkson’s past controversies, and think he really does represent them in every way.

https://metro.co.uk/2023/10/28/feeding-m.text:
Carrying two plates of food into the living room, I placed them in front of my two children, Theo, five, and Immy, four. ‘Dinner is served,’ I announced.
‘Yay, hot dogs!’ Theo cheered, grabbing a finger bun before turning back to the television.
Sitting down on the sofa, I sighed. When I was pregnant – even when the kids were younger – this was a scene I never imagined I’d see.
Serving up processed meat in white bread, not a vegetable in sight, which my children scoffed mindlessly, their eyes glued to the latest episode of Muppet Babies.
Hardly a scene from a parenting manual.
But, to be frank, I’ve long since given up on the idea of being a perfect parent. Now, I’ve finally accepted that being a ‘good enough’ parent is good enough for me.
When I first found out I was pregnant, my husband Tom and I had high expectations about what we’d be like as ‘mum and dad’.
We agreed we would always have our evening meal around the dinner table together, something home cooked and wholesome – which we’d enjoy while catching up on our days.
We would go for long walks round the park on weekends, take our children to museums and the library. We’d read them books, limit screen-time and spend our afternoons playing family-friendly games.
Don’t get me wrong, we never believed we could be perfect parents. I mean, does such a thing even exist?
But that certainly wasn’t going to stop us trying.
‘You never argue or shout, do you?’ my sister asked in amazement when she had come to stay for a few days.
Famous last words, eh?
Because of course, that kind of attentiveness and striving for perfection just isn’t sustainable in any aspect of life.
For me, it came to a head when we relocated from London back to my home town in the north of England.
It was, hands down, the most stressful thing I have ever done and, as we organised removal companies and completion dates, we just didn’t have the time to be at our children’s beck and call the way we’d always tried to be before.
Then, of course, there was the emotional toll as well, which frayed our nerves.
‘Can you please just wait a minute?’ I snapped sharply at Theo one night, as he tugged at my sleeve for the tenth time, asking me to get his Spiderman from upstairs.
Looking into his big brown eyes, guilt immediately overwhelmed me. ‘I’m sorry, sweetheart,’ I said, bending down to give him a hug. ‘Mammy is just really busy.’
As tears filled my eyes, it suddenly struck me. It was just too much, trying to be a model employee, the perfect parent, the friend I had always been… the burden was crippling me.
I couldn’t do it all and, by expecting myself to, I was just setting myself up for failure.
When Theo was born, he refused to latch on – making breastfeeding impossible. I’d stay up after he went to bed to express milk so when he awoke in the middle of the night, there would be some ready and waiting for him. Then I’d set my alarm to do the same at 5.30am each morning.

When he got older and Immy came along, Tom and I did everything they asked, as soon as they asked – racing to get drinks, stopping whatever we were doing to listen to them when they had something to say and always working our weekends around playdates and parties.
I was just one person – a working mum with only so many hours in the day to juggle all of the plates that living in today’s society brings.
I could only do my best and give up completely trying to get it exactly right, each and every single time. Slowly but surely, my mindset changed.
If my work ran over and I didn’t have time to cook a chilli or a spaghetti Bolognese from scratch, then it wasn’t the worst thing if I just stuck a pizza in the oven.
If the kids ended up spending a Sunday morning watching two films in a row, while Tom and I sorted out the house, I didn’t have to beat myself up over it.
It turns out, there is even a theory, called ‘good enough parenting’, put forward by UK paediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott in the 1950s, which states that actually sometimes it is better for your child if you ‘fail’ them at some points, and aren’t always immediately available and responsive to their needs.
Of course, this isn’t referring to neglect or not looking after your children properly. Their physical and emotional needs still need to be met.
Rather, it’s more about realising that, once they’re passed the baby stage, you can ask your children to wait for a minute, rather than jumping to attention whenever they ask for something. And realising that actually parents can sometimes make mistakes – and that is OK.
Children, he said, can learn to experience that tears, sadness and anger are all part of life – and that it is good for them to experience certain levels of frustration.
Thank goodness for that!
So if you’re feeling overwhelmed or upset or frustrated when you lose your temper or you can’t immediately get them their third glass of water in 15 minutes – please, don’t.

https://metro.co.uk/2023/10/27/im-a-sex-.text:
As a sex writer (hell, as a woman) I’m used to people judging my private life.
But there’s a limit to what I can accept and earlier this week, I was reminded of that very limit when a random troll commented on an X post of my article.
He said my parents must be ashamed of me because of my job.
He added that sharing my sexual experiences publicly must mean that I’m ‘easy’, and others have expressed that they think I probably f**k every man I know.
How delightful.
I’d love to tell you that this is the first occasion where I’ve received a nasty comment. It isn’t – and it won’t be the last, either.
Most of the time, I can shake it off.
The thing is, I am determined to bring sex out of the bedroom and into our everyday lives for everyone’s benefit, and you can’t create real change without taking the good with the bad.
Shaming those who dare to be sex-positive – whether offline or online, in public or in private – could do more harm than good.
And turning sex into something shameful or secret only makes it harder for people to access help, should they need it.
But dealing with keyboard warriors is one thing – it’s tougher when this type of judgment happens in real life.

I was furious and went to bed (by myself), leaving them to drink in our living room.
Fast-forward to my 30s and there was another incident.
A friend confessed that she had contemplated the future of our friendship because she felt I brought up my dating and sex life ‘too often’.
As you might’ve guessed, I was single and she was not. Our lifestyles didn’t align, but that doesn’t mean my stories or concerns were any less valid than hers.
This can happen quite often with friends who are in different stages of dating, but that’s another column.
My friend and I talked it out and she apologised profusely, but her words stung for a long time afterwards.
It’s not just (some) women who appear perturbed by my openness about sex.
Long before I was a journalist, there were men who believed I was promiscuous or ‘up for a shag’ purely because I have a flirty character. Which isn’t the case.
Just because I like sex, it does not mean I am always horny and interested in any penis at my disposal.
When it comes to sex, women in particular are doomed regardless of what we do.
As an example, a former long-term partner loved that we had an exciting sex life, but he still got very jealous if I mentioned any of my past sexual experiences.
It’s not like I rubbed my exes in his face – that’s bad behaviour – but I believe that you can learn from the past, and there are certain details, emotional and physical, that can be helpful to know.
For instance, perhaps you’ve suffered trauma that impacts how you feel about sex or maybe it’s just a case of what you don’t and do like, both positive and negative.
Meanwhile other men have told me that the idea a woman has slept with anyone other than them is off-putting.
We are to remain virginal saints (but still give good blowjobs, apparently).
If it bothers you that a woman is taking ownership of her sex life, ask yourself why that is – are you brave enough to face the answer?
I can already hear the trolls shouting, ‘well if you don’t want to be treated this way, stop having, writing or talking about sex’.
Playing devil’s advocate for a moment, I get it.
I am telling you the ins and outs of my escapades in a public forum, but I do this in the hopes that it will lift stigma and offer a safe, sex-positive space to discuss sex, as well as make you laugh.
Personal attacks are inexcusable.
Besides, there are important issues that we must talk about, such as consent, sexual health, safety during sex and pleasure, to name but a few.
On a positive note, I’ve had some lovely experiences too.
An acquaintance once reached out to ask for my opinion when she was having trouble with her boyfriend and wanted to reignite their sex life.
Another felt self-conscious about not having had sex for a long time, and was put at ease when they were told this is nothing to be ashamed of.
Someone else asked for masturbation tips because she struggled with having orgasms and it was affecting her mental wellbeing.
I feel incredibly privileged and proud that these people were comfortable in speaking to me about these things.
And this is exactly why I won’t stop talking or writing about sex.
If someone is bothered by my sex-positive attitude or sex life, that’s their issue.
Plus, I’m stubborn and I was raised by two strong people who taught me the value of my voice.
And yes, they’re damn proud of me.

From the minute I wake-up, it’s all systems go.
Knocking on bedroom doors after alarm-clocks have been ignored. Juggling various breakfast orders from porridge to pancakes. Then packing the lunches from what I like to call ‘Dad’s pop-up sandwich bar’.
It never stops, but I wouldn’t change it for the world. I absolutely love being a dad.
I always wanted a big family. I even ended my wedding speech with a toast: ‘Now it’s time to have lots of bambinos!’
But for the longest time it didn’t look like becoming parents would be on the cards for my wife, Siobhan, and I. We were devastated.
Then, in the space of 18 months, we went from no children to five. Yes, really. I’m still in shock.
We faced challenges trying to conceive right from the off and I found it particularly hard seeing Siobhan’s deep disappointment each month. But come the start of the next month, she’d be full of hope again.
Both of us were just waiting for our family to truly start.
It seemed like everyone around us was falling pregnant with ease. While we wanted to be happy for our friends, it was always tinged with sadness for what we couldn’t have.
The longer we tried and failed, the sadder we both felt.
Not ready to give up, we embarked on fertility treatment. At the start, we were both positive – doctors even congratulated my wife on the number of eggs she’d produced after weeks of injections.
But just one day later, we were told that none had fertilised. It was heartbreaking.
Over the next six years we went for a second, third and fourth round of IVF – but still nothing.
At this point, a decision had to be made. We both agreed that being parents was more important than having our own children. And we were conscious of getting older. Alongside IVF, we had been considering and exploring adoption.
We said a painful goodbye to our fertility journey, and instead turned our hopes for a family through adoption.
It was something I’d always been interested in exploring. As a children and families social worker, I was only too aware of how many children there are waiting to be adopted. I had also spent time in my late teens working a Romanian orphanage, which had a profound impact on me.
After a long period of research, talks, training and an intense, but necessarily thorough, assessment, we were approved by the adoption panel.
I’ll be honest, at first, we spent a lot of time looking through profiles of children searching for a one-day old baby and a nine-month-old so that we could mould them in our own image. We initially saw adoption as a direct replacement for our infertility.
Then we came across a near five-year-old boy and his two-year-old sister, and they changed everything. We knew instantly we’d be a great match for each other, it was such a strong gut feeling.
We knew we’d be expected to tell the social worker and approval panel why we wanted them and so, we fashioned something together, but the simple truth was that we’d fallen in love.
The morning we were due to meet them at their foster parents’, we arrived two hours early, full of nervous anticipation. We were worried that they might not like us, we were rehearsing what to say and how to react.

As we walked towards the house, my heart was racing, my hands were sweating, and I was deadly silent.
Each step closer to the front door felt like a monumental leap into a new chapter of the lives we had wanted for so long.
When the front door swung open, our son ran towards me and clutched onto my leg. I held back the tears as I caught Siobhan’s eye.
Our daughter, meanwhile, slowly appeared from behind the foster carer’s legs, quiet and shy. But she soon came to life when we got the colouring pens out.
That was it. We became parents in an instant.
It was full-on initially, with both of them being very demanding, physically and emotionally. During the first week, we went to bed at the same time as them – we were exhausted!
Gradually, though, we settled into family life. There were moments of chaos, laughter, and the kind of mess that only children can create.
Our son was a constant presence, as he found it difficult to be alone. But with time, he grew in confidence.
Thankfully my wife had taken a year’s adoption leave to give us time to all to settle in together.
But just as she was planning to return to work, amazingly she discovered that she was pregnant. We knew that balancing two kids and a new baby would be tricky, but we were just so overcome with joy to be growing our family.
I was away in Birmingham just about to speak at a conference when she booked herself in for an early scan, worried that things didn’t feel right.
I told her to text me with updates but nothing could have prepared me for what she’d say next.
‘They’ve found two, and possibly a third, I’m just waiting for an enhanced scan,’ she wrote.
I started to panic, fearing she was having a miscarriage.
‘No babe,’ she replied. ‘They have found two heart beats, and possibly a third!’
It still wasn’t sinking in, so she wrote, in all capital letters, ‘IT MEANS THREE BABIES MARK!’
How I held it together through my presentation is still beyond me.
At 32 weeks, the triplets were born in good health. Any parent will tell you that the flood of emotions that comes with the arrival of a new child is something that can’t easily be put into words, but to have three new babies was something else entirely – I was overwhelmed and overjoyed.
As my wife recovered in hospital with our three new bundles, I drove home to share the news with our two children, crying the whole way.
Callum and Gracie were waiting expectantly at the door when I arrived, and were disappointed when I got out of the car alone – ‘Where are they?’, they asked!
After I explained why they had to stay in the hospital, being premature, they excitedly got in the car later to visit them, chatting in the back together talking about what they were going to do with their new brothers and sisters.
I was now a father of five. Madness.
From that moment, life has never been the same. Callum is now 17, Gracie is 14 and the triplets – Hector, Aoife and Raffie – are aged 10.
We’re now a mad house of nine, including the two dogs, and it is all wonderfully vibrant and full of life.
We’d strongly encourage others to adopt, both as a first option, and in response to infertility. It has brought us immense joy and fulfilment.
I feel truly blessed, and thankful for every single one of my children.

Vile. Sub-human. Sickening.
Those are the ableist slurs used to describe me after I landed my first big television job in a Maltesers ad in 2016.
One light-hearted 30-second commercial had people on social media tagging me in hurtful memes and making fun of my disability – brittle bones disease, which is a rare genetic condition that means I’m of petite stature so I use a wheelchair full-time.
Having the opportunity to highlight incidents like these is why National Hate Crime Awareness Week is so important.
I always knew that I wanted a career in the spotlight. I guess it’s just in my DNA. In fact, I vividly remember being in my last year at primary school and sharing these ambitions.
I was sitting in the sports hall in my fluffy red and brown powerchair – with two pigtails and wearing oversized multi-coloured glasses that drowned my face (think Deirdre Barlow from Coronation Street) – when my support assistant at the time and a class teacher asked me what I would like to be when I was older.
Without hesitation, I proudly said: ‘After high school, I need to go to college then university and I want to either become a teacher or, if that doesn’t work out, an actress’. Perhaps I was manifesting but – lo and behold – that’s pretty much the path I took.
Little did I know that putting myself out there so publicly as a disabled woman with a voice and eagerness to help change the world for the better would put me in such a vulnerable position.
This decision has led me to experience some of the most awful hate and ableist abuse, which impacted my sense of self-worth and negatively affected my mental health. It’s not always so overt as the fallout from my Maltesers ad, either.
I feel it in everyday microaggressions, like when people tell me they feel sorry for me because I’m in a wheelchair. Or inspiration porn of things like a picture – mostly of a disabled kid doing something ‘unexpected’ – and the slogan: ‘If they can do it, what’s your excuse?’
But sometimes it can be more sinister. Just before the pandemic, I experienced sexual assault after somebody weaponised my wheelchair to forcibly sexually abuse me.
It was the most terrifying moment of my life because I felt so vulnerable and scared.
If you want to be a friend and ally to disabled folk you need to – first and foremost – educate yourself and those around you
Despite that, I didn’t report it. The reason being, I couldn’t envision having potentially ableist police officers in my home who – due to their own unconscious bias – might see disabled people as asexual or unattractive and therefore not susceptible to something as heinous as sexual assault.
I couldn’t face not being believed. My fears aren’t unfounded either. I’ve often had people assume I couldn’t have sex or be in a relationship, or that the only people who would find me attractive are those who want to fetishise me.
My own personal stories are just a drop in the ocean when it comes to disability hate crime. And, of course, you don’t have to be on television or an influencer in the public eye to experience this.
According to disability organisation, Scope, hate crime directed at our community can consist of: physical attacks – such as assault, damage to property or arson – attacks on assistance dogs, threat of attack – including offensive letters, abusive or obscene telephone calls, texts or intimidation – harassment, bullying and abuse at school, online or in the workplace.
New Research from non-profit support provider Dimensions has found that a fifth of the public have laughed at someone, called someone names or avoided talking to someone because of their learning disability or autism. Shockingly, 6% of UK adults admit to having physically hurt someone because of their learning disability or autism, which is the equivalent to 3.6million people.

You might not be part of that 6% stat but if you turn a blind eye, you are part of the problem.
I am often left saddened and frustrated by the sheer lack of outrage and action taken when it comes to disability hate. Do I want a witch hunt and my allies to become vigilantes? Absolutely not, as I believe hate just adds to more hate.
However, I will no longer stand for apathy. If you want to be a friend and ally to disabled folk you need to – first and foremost – educate yourself and those around you.
Are you using ableist terminology and slurs? Are you also holding your children accountable if you hear them using degrading terms? Do you even understand what ableism means and how it impacts the lives of disabled people?
If the answer to that latter question is ‘no’, educate yourself on the history of ableism until you understand how deep-rooted some of these ideologies are.
I mean, it wasn’t too long ago that we were given the title of ‘untermensch’ (meaning sub-human) during the Third Reich and the systemic ableism surrounds our society like a toxic smog. Whether or not you can see it, it’s still there.
Above all, I want you to start to begin the tough work of uncovering your own hidden ableism biases. To do this, you need to first leave your ego at the door.
If a disabled person calls out ableism, please be respectful and understand that we are all learning and it is never too late to unlearn and relearn.
